title: Named themes beyond light/dark: muted, warm palettes (gruvbox, sepia)
description:
Andy finds both current themes harsh: "sometimes the stark white on black vibrates in my eyes, I need something more muted, like gruvbox or something sepia themed."

That is exactly what the values do. application.tailwind.css sets light to --color-background hsl(0 0% 100%) against --color-foreground hsl(0 0% 3.9%), and .dark inverts it to hsl(0 0% 3.9%) on hsl(0 0% 98%). Pure greyscale at close to maximum contrast, with no hue anywhere in the neutrals. Gruvbox and sepia families differ on both axes: lower contrast, and warm hue carried through the backgrounds and text rather than only in accents.

Current architecture, which is better suited to this than expected:
- The palette is fully tokenised. The @theme block defines about 21 semantic --color-* variables and the .dark block in @layer base overrides the same set. A third palette is a third override block, not a rewrite.
- Escape hatches are rare: 23 hardcoded Tailwind palette utilities across 11 files, all semantic status colours (text-green-600 for success, bg-yellow-50 and border-yellow-200 for warnings). No structural chrome is hardcoded.

Two structural limits to fix first:
- ThemeContext.tsx types Theme as "light" | "dark" | "system" and applies it by adding or removing a single "dark" class on documentElement. resolvedTheme is typed "light" | "dark". There is no room for a named theme.
- Theme is persisted only to localStorage under nibbler-theme, even though a server-side theme preference already exists (permitted at preferences_controller.rb:44, defaulted to "system" at line 72) and nothing reads or writes it. So theme does not follow the user across devices, unlike accent_hue, which does.

Open design question for the children: with N themes, what does "system" mean? Recommended answer is that system picks between a designated light theme and a designated dark theme, both user-selectable, rather than being a third value.
close_reason:
All six children closed. Andy can now pick Gruvbox Dark, Gruvbox Light or Sepia in Settings, and the choice persists to his account.

Children:
- ttrb-w6ob (c3fcba6) registry: a theme is { id, name, base }, applied as data-theme=<id> plus the .dark class for dark-base themes
- ttrb-nkhp (9bfff5f) Gruvbox Dark, Gruvbox Light, Sepia authored as [data-theme] blocks
- ttrb-lyo3 (5fb9f95) Tailwind dark: variant follows the class instead of prefers-color-scheme
- ttrb-g18k (591873c) selection persists to the account; localStorage demoted to a first-paint cache
- ttrb-1im8 (72030ca) swatch picker deriving its colours from the registry via nested data-theme, so a new palette needs no component edit
- ttrb-x7fn (a19e02f) theme-unsafe colour audit: 19 hardcoded utilities across 7 files replaced, plus two regression guards

Against the complaint that started it ("the stark white on black vibrates in my eyes, I need something more muted, like gruvbox or something sepia themed"): body-text contrast is 19.80:1 on stock Light and 18.97:1 on stock Dark, against 10.67 Gruvbox Dark, 10.30 Gruvbox Light, 8.65 Sepia. Roughly half, all still clearing AA.

Three defects were found that predate the epic and were fixed inside it: Tailwind dark: utilities followed the OS rather than the app theme at nine call sites; stock Light failed AA at 4.35:1 for muted-foreground on muted (token nudged 45.1% -> 44%, now 4.54); and the TTS/search highlight rules paired white against a fixed-lightness accent ramp, giving 1.51:1 at hue 60 and failing at 16 of 24 hues on dark bases. All now 4.95:1 worst case across the wheel.

Deliberately NOT a child, and still open: ttrb-x7zz (P1) — --color-destructive measures 1.98:1 on Dark and 3.76:1 on Light as text, in 29 places. It predates the epic, is independent of the warm palettes (the three hand-authored ones pass), and fixing it changes how the destructive Button looks on the stock palettes, which is Andy design call rather than an audit finding.

NOT VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION. Everything above is the test suite plus Chromium measurement on this machine. 274 e2e, 895 vitest, 593 Ruby runs, all passing.

title: Generalize ThemeContext from a binary dark class to a named-theme registry
description:
Current behavior
app/javascript/contexts/ThemeContext.tsx hardcodes the binary:

  type Theme = "light" | "dark" | "system"
  resolvedTheme: "light" | "dark"

and applies it by root.classList.add("dark") / remove("dark"). getResolvedTheme collapses "system" to one of two values. Nothing can express a third palette.

The CSS side matches: application.tailwind.css puts the light palette in @theme and overrides it under a single .dark selector inside @layer base.

Expected behavior
A registry of named themes. Each theme has an id, a display name, a light-or-dark base (so the system setting and any is-dark logic still work), and a CSS class. Applying a theme swaps one class on documentElement rather than toggling a boolean.

Implementation notes
- Replace the single "dark" class toggle with removing any previously applied theme class and adding the new one. Keep "dark" as the class name for the dark theme so the existing .dark selectors, including .dark .tts-word-active in the stylesheet, keep working. Any theme with a dark base likely needs to carry the dark class too, or those selectors need generalising to a data attribute.
- Consider a data-theme attribute on documentElement instead of, or alongside, classes. It reads better and avoids class collisions, but every existing .dark selector would need updating, so weigh that.
- "system" resolves to a designated light theme and a designated dark theme rather than being a theme itself. Default those to the current light and dark so behaviour is unchanged for anyone who does not pick.
- Unknown or removed theme ids stored from an earlier version must fall back cleanly rather than leaving the app unstyled.

Affected files
- app/javascript/contexts/ThemeContext.tsx
- app/assets/stylesheets/application.tailwind.css (the .dark block becomes one of several theme blocks)
- a new theme registry module, likely app/javascript/lib/themes.ts alongside accentColors.ts

Acceptance criteria
- Adding a theme means adding a registry entry and a CSS block, with no changes to ThemeContext.
- Existing light, dark and system behaviour is unchanged for a user who has never picked a theme.
- A stored theme id that no longer exists falls back to system without a broken render.
- Vitest coverage for resolution, class swapping, and the unknown-id fallback.
close_reason: ThemeContext now resolves through a named-theme registry (app/javascript/lib/themes.ts). data-theme selects the palette, the dark class marks the base. Light/dark/system behaviour unchanged; unknown stored ids fall back to system. Verified by adding and removing a throwaway third palette with no ThemeContext change.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Filed ttrb-lyo3: Tailwind's dark: variant compiles to @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark), not the .dark class, so nine call sites already ignore a pinned theme. Pre-existing, made more visible by the epic. Added as a child of ttrb-xj40.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Commit c3fcba6: theme registry landed.

app/javascript/lib/themes.ts holds the registry (id, display name, light-or-dark base) plus pure resolution and a DOM apply helper. Applying writes data-theme=<id> on <html> and adds the dark class when base is dark, so the palette and the is-it-dark fact stay independent. The stylesheet palette block moved from .dark to [data-theme="dark"]; .dark .tts-word-active and .dark .search-mark keep their selector and now match any future dark palette.

system resolves through DEFAULT_SYSTEM_THEMES, and resolveTheme takes that pair as an argument so ttrb-x7fn can make it a user preference without touching resolution. An unregistered stored id resolves as if it were system. resolvedTheme keeps its light|dark type, now meaning the applied palette's base, so FeedSidebar's isDark branches survive new palettes. PreferencesPanel derives its options from THEMES.

Empirical check of the first acceptance criterion: added a throwaway 'probe-warm' theme as a registry entry plus a [data-theme="probe-warm"] block, nothing else. It appeared in the picker, painted rgb(42,41,39) on rgb(228,221,201) from its own block, and carried the dark class. Reverted after; tree is clean against c3fcba6.

Tests: vitest 790 passed / 45 files (was 760 / 43); Playwright settings+smoke 46 passed; Ruby 489 runs, 1439 assertions, 0 failures. Two of the new Playwright cases guard the registry-to-stylesheet seam that vitest cannot see.

title: Theme preference is localStorage-only while an unused server-side theme preference already exists
description:
Current behavior
ThemeContext.tsx persists the theme to localStorage under nibbler-theme (THEME_STORAGE_KEY, written in setTheme at line 72, read in getStoredTheme at line 29). Nothing sends it to the server.

Meanwhile the server already has the preference. It is in the permitted list at app/controllers/api/v1/preferences_controller.rb:44 and defaulted to "system" at line 72, and api.ts:191 types it as theme: string on the preferences object. Nothing in app/javascript reads or writes it. PreferencesPanel.tsx:101 uses useTheme() from the context, not the preference.

So there is a theme column that is written by nobody and read by nobody, sitting next to accent_hue, which IS driven through PreferencesContext (applyAccentColors at PreferencesContext.tsx:61). Two adjacent appearance settings, two different persistence mechanisms, and the one with server support does not use it.

Consequences
- Theme does not follow the user to another browser or device; accent colour does.
- Clearing site data resets the theme but not the accent.
- The dead column will confuse whoever next reads the preferences list.

Expected behavior
One persistence path for appearance settings. Move theme onto the existing preference, matching how accent_hue works, and treat localStorage as a pre-hydration cache only if a flash of the wrong theme is a problem.

Note on flash-of-wrong-theme: reading from localStorage synchronously before first paint is why it is there. If theme moves to a server round trip, the initial render can flash the default before preferences arrive. Keep a localStorage mirror written on change and read on boot, with the server value as the source of truth once loaded, or render an inline script in the layout that applies the class before React mounts.

Affected files
- app/javascript/contexts/ThemeContext.tsx
- app/javascript/contexts/PreferencesContext.tsx
- app/javascript/components/PreferencesPanel.tsx
- app/views/layouts/application.html.erb (only if the pre-paint script route is taken)

Acceptance criteria
- Changing the theme in one browser and loading the app in another shows the same theme.
- No flash of the wrong theme on load.
- The theme preference is genuinely read and written, or it is removed from the permitted list and defaults.
close_reason: Theme now persists to the existing server preference; localStorage is the first-paint cache. Commit 591873c.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Commit 591873c: theme moved onto the existing server preference. ThemeContext.setTheme now applies, caches and PATCHes {theme}; PreferencesContext hands the loaded value to a new adoptServerTheme and adopts a cache-only theme once when the account still reports the default "system". localStorage stays as the first-paint cache (ThemeProvider paints above PreferencesProvider). Catching test: PreferencesPanel.theme.test.tsx, 4 of 6 fail against the previous code; e2e reload test now clears the cache first. Rails 593/1835/0/0, vitest 879 passed (49 files), e2e 266 passed 5 skipped, rubocop 202 files no offenses.

title: Author the gruvbox and sepia palettes as theme token blocks
description:
With the theme registry in place, add the palettes Andy actually asked for. Both are answers to the same complaint: the current pair are pure greyscale at close to maximum contrast, which vibrates.

Themes to add
- Gruvbox dark: the standard warm dark palette, background around #282828, foreground around #ebdbb2. Notably lower contrast than the current dark theme and warm rather than neutral.
- Gruvbox light: background around #fbf1c7, foreground around #3c3836.
- Sepia: warm paper background, brown-black text. Lower contrast than the current light theme.

Andy said "gruvbox or something sepia themed", so treat the exact set as a proposal and check before building all four. Gruvbox dark plus sepia may be the whole ask.

Each theme fills the same token set the .dark block already covers: background, foreground, card, card-foreground, popover, popover-foreground, primary, primary-foreground, secondary, secondary-foreground, muted, muted-foreground, accent, accent-foreground, destructive, destructive-foreground, border, input, ring.

Interaction with the accent hue system
accentColors.ts applyAccentColors writes --color-accent-primary and friends as INLINE styles on documentElement (root.style.setProperty). Inline styles beat any class-based rule, so a theme CANNOT set its own accent colours by declaring them in its CSS block; the stored accent_hue will always win. Decide deliberately:
- Let the user hue keep overriding, so themes define only the neutral palette. Simplest, and the accent slider keeps meaning what it means.
- Give each theme a default hue applied when the theme is selected, still user-overridable afterwards. Gruvbox has its own accent identity, so this is the better fit for it.
Whichever is chosen, note it in accentColors.ts so the inline-style precedence is not rediscovered the hard way.

Affected files
- app/assets/stylesheets/application.tailwind.css
- the theme registry module from the sibling bead
- app/javascript/lib/accentColors.ts (only if themes carry default hues)

Acceptance criteria
- Each theme defines every token in the set; no token falls through to the light default and produces a white patch.
- Text on background meets WCAG AA at normal body size in each theme. Muted foreground on muted background is the pair most likely to fail, so check that one explicitly.
- The 23 hardcoded status colours (green success, yellow and amber warning) are legible on every new background.
- Screenshots of the entry list, entry content, sidebar and a dialog in each theme.
close_reason: Added Gruvbox Dark, Gruvbox Light and Sepia as [data-theme] palette blocks plus registry entries (commit 9bfff5f). Body text 10.67 / 10.30 / 8.65:1 against the greyscale pair's 19.8 and 19.0; muted-foreground clears AA on both muted and background in all three. Accent hue left under user control, precedence documented in accentColors.ts. Two browser-side guards added: palette-block completeness read off the compiled stylesheet, and a computed-contrast floor. Built the three themes the description named; a dark sepia was not built.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Commit 9bfff5f: added gruvbox-dark, gruvbox-light and sepia as [data-theme] blocks plus registry entries. Measured in Chrome (Playwright, after settling): body text 10.67 / 10.30 / 8.65; muted-fg on muted 5.45 / 4.82 / 5.12; muted-fg on background 6.78 / 5.79 / 5.70; destructive text on background 4.59 / 7.48 / 6.36. All 19 tokens defined in each block. Accent hue left user-controlled (option 1 in the description); precedence documented in accentColors.ts.

title: Replace the light/dark/system select with a theme picker showing palette swatches
description:
PreferencesPanel.tsx:119 renders a Theme label over a select bound to useTheme(), with three fixed options. With a theme registry it needs to list N themes and show what each one looks like, since names like gruvbox mean nothing to someone who has not seen it.

Requirements
- List every registered theme, grouped or labelled by light and dark base so the list stays scannable as it grows.
- A swatch per theme showing at minimum background, foreground, muted and border, so the choice is visible without applying it.
- Keep System as its own option, resolving to the designated light and dark themes.
- Applying is immediate, as the accent hue slider already is (PreferencesPanel.tsx:157 calls applyAccentColors on change).

Sits directly below the accent colour control, which is the other appearance setting, so the two should read as one group.

Affected files
- app/javascript/components/PreferencesPanel.tsx
- the theme registry module from the sibling bead

Acceptance criteria
- Every registered theme is selectable and previewed without being applied.
- Selecting a theme applies it immediately and persists it.
- Adding a theme to the registry makes it appear here with no change to this component.
- The control is usable at mobile width.
close_reason: Theme select replaced by a swatch picker: radio group of cards, each swatch scoped by data-theme so the stylesheet supplies its colours; new [data-theme="light"] block so Light previews correctly; System shown as the two palettes it switches between. Commit 72030ca.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Heads-up from ttrb-g18k (591873c): theme persistence moved into ThemeContext.setTheme, which now applies the palette, writes the nibbler-theme first-paint cache, and PATCHes {theme} to the preferences API. The PreferencesPanel JSX was left untouched, so the swatch picker only has to keep calling setTheme(selection) with a value from THEMES (or "system") and persistence comes with it. Do not write localStorage directly and do not call updatePreference("theme", ...); either one bypasses half of it. Reading the current selection is still useTheme().theme, not preferences.theme.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Commit 72030ca: PreferencesPanel's theme Select replaced by ThemePicker.tsx, a radio group of swatch cards.

Swatch derivation: each swatch element sets data-theme="<id>" on itself and paints with the semantic utilities (bg-background, bg-foreground, bg-muted-foreground, bg-muted, border-border). The [data-theme] blocks in application.tailwind.css are bare attribute selectors, so they match a nested element as readily as <html>; the cascade supplies the colours and no colour value appears in TS. Adding a registry entry plus its stylesheet block puts a correct swatch here with no edit to the component.

This required adding a [data-theme="light"] block. Light was the :root/@theme default with no block of its own, so a nested data-theme="light" inherited the page's current palette and the Light swatch showed whatever theme was applied. The light values are now written twice (@theme for the :root fallback and Tailwind's utility generation, plus the palette block); a new e2e test reads the compiled stylesheet and fails if the two disagree, and the existing block-coverage test now expects a block for every registered id including light.

System: no single swatch. Drawn as the two palettes DEFAULT_SYSTEM_THEMES names, side by side, with 'Switches with your device setting, between Light and Dark' built from the same pair (aria-hidden, wired by aria-describedby so the option's accessible name stays 'System'). Showing the currently-resolved palette would read as a sixth fixed choice.

Persistence untouched: setTheme(selection) only, current selection read from useTheme().theme. No localStorage, no updatePreference.

Accessibility: role=radiogroup labelled by a span (not a Label with a dangling htmlFor), role=group per base, native radios whose labels wrap them. Tab reaches the checked radio, ArrowDown moves and selects. ThemePicker.test.tsx asserts all of it via getByRole, including that no label[for] in the subtree points at a missing id.

Measured in Chromium, swatch vs the page under that palette (background / foreground / muted-foreground / muted / border), all five identical:
  light        255,255,255 | 10,10,10   | 115,115,115 | 245,245,245 | 229,229,229
  dark          10,10,10   | 250,250,250| 163,163,163 |  38,38,38   |  38,38,38
  gruvbox-dark  43,40,38   | 235,219,178| 189,175,147 |  59,55,53   |  74,68,64
  gruvbox-light 251,240,198|  59,55,53  | 101,91,83   | 235,219,178 | 217,202,171
  sepia        244,236,215 |  75,63,53  | 106,89,68   | 234,224,200 | 220,208,183

Suites: bin/rails test 593/1835/0/0; npm run test:run 891 passed / 50 files (was 879/49, +12 ThemePicker); npm run test:e2e 269 passed 5 skipped (was 266/5, +3); rubocop 202 files no offenses.

title: Audit theme-unsafe colors: hardcoded status utilities and the white in .dark .tts-word-active
description:
Before shipping new palettes, verify nothing renders a colour that only works against the two existing backgrounds.

Known offenders
- 23 hardcoded Tailwind palette utilities across 11 tsx files, all semantic status colours: text-green-600, text-green-500, text-green-400, text-green-700, text-green-800, bg-green-50, border-green-200, text-yellow-600, text-yellow-700, text-yellow-800, bg-yellow-50, border-yellow-200, text-amber-500. These are success and warning states. bg-green-50 and bg-yellow-50 are near-white fills that will glow against a gruvbox or sepia background.
- application.tailwind.css .dark .tts-word-active hardcodes color: white against --color-accent-primary. Any dark-base theme inherits that rule if it carries the dark class, and white may be wrong for a warm palette.

Scope
Small: 23 occurrences plus one CSS rule. The decision is what to replace them with, not how much work it is.

Options
- Add semantic success and warning tokens (--color-success, --color-success-foreground, --color-warning, --color-warning-foreground) to the token set every theme defines, and swap the utilities for them. Correct, and makes the token set self-documenting about what a theme must supply.
- Leave them as literal Tailwind colours and accept that they read as slightly foreign in warm themes. Defensible for two states that are meant to stand out.

The first is recommended, since the token set is what a new theme author has to fill in and a silent hardcoded colour is exactly what they cannot discover.

Also add a lint or test guard so the next hardcoded palette utility is caught rather than found by eye. The existing keyboardShortcuts catalog uses an exhaustive-map trick to make drift a compile error; a similar guard for theme tokens is worth considering.

Affected files
- the 11 tsx files carrying the status utilities
- app/assets/stylesheets/application.tailwind.css (token set, .dark .tts-word-active)

Acceptance criteria
- Success and warning states are legible and in keeping in every theme.
- No component renders a background or text colour that is not derived from a theme token, other than deliberately documented exceptions.
- A guard exists that fails when a new hardcoded palette utility is added, or a decision not to add one is recorded here.
close_reason: Audit complete (a19e02f). Semantic --color-success/--color-warning added to all five palettes and swapped in for 19 hardcoded utilities; OpmlPanel's near-white cards now token tints; the literal white removed from all four accent-highlight rules (hue-stable at 4.95:1 worst, was 1.51:1); Light's muted-foreground raised to 44% so the contrast test covers all five palettes with no exemption; NibblerLogo and ui/badge de-whited. Two guards added. --color-destructive left under the bar deliberately and filed as ttrb-x7zz.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Measured against the three new palettes (ttrb-nkhp, commit 9bfff5f), in Chrome via Playwright. Nothing is plainly unreadable, but two things are now quantified:

1. Status utilities as ICON colour on the light-base backgrounds. Contrast vs background, gruvbox-light / sepia (Light for reference): text-green-500 1.94 / 1.88 (2.22), text-amber-500 1.87 / 1.81 (2.13), text-yellow-600 2.57 / 2.49 (2.94), text-green-600 2.82 / 2.73 (3.22). So the warm backgrounds cost roughly 0.1-0.4, and green-500/amber-500 were already under the 3:1 non-text minimum on plain white. Pre-existing, mildly worsened. On gruvbox-dark they are all fine (4.55 to 6.86).

2. OpmlPanel's near-white fills are the real offender and are worse on a dark base than a warm light one. app/javascript/components/OpmlPanel.tsx lines 149-153 (bg-yellow-50 border-yellow-200 text-yellow-800/700) and 204-208 (bg-green-50 border-green-200 text-green-800/700) have no dark: variant at all, so they render as a bright near-white card on the existing Dark theme too. Warm light themes only make them look foreign; the dark themes make them glare.

3. .tts-word-active and .search-mark are unchanged by the new palettes: they follow the user's accent hue, so at the default hue 210 they paint a cool blue patch (rgb(226,235,243) fill, rgb(22,89,156) text, 5.92:1) on a cream page. Legible, but chromatically foreign to gruvbox/sepia. The .dark .tts-word-active white-on-accent case measures 4.06:1 on both dark and gruvbox-dark - identical, since it uses only accent vars.

Also worth folding in here: the stock Light theme's own --color-muted-foreground on --color-muted is 4.35:1, under AA. The e2e contrast assertion added in ttrb-nkhp excludes Light for that reason.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Follow-up from ttrb-lyo3 (commit 5fb9f95), which made the `dark:` variant key off the .dark class instead of prefers-color-scheme. This changes which of the numbers above a reader actually sees, and it does not fix anything on this ticket.

FeedOrganizer.tsx:96 is the one status utility in the list with a dark: variant: `text-green-600 dark:text-green-400`. Before 5fb9f95 the variant followed the OS, so a reader on a dark-preference OS with a light palette pinned got green-400 on a light background. Measured in Chromium (canvas-resolved sRGB, WCAG formula): green-400 rgb(5,223,114) sits at 1.78:1 on Light, 1.56:1 on Gruvbox Light, 1.51:1 on Sepia. Effectively invisible, and worse than any figure recorded above.

After the fix those readers get green-600 rgb(0,166,62): 3.22 / 2.82 / 2.73:1, exactly the numbers in the comment above. So the audit's recorded ratios are now what everyone sees rather than what only an OS-agreeing reader saw, and green-600 on the two warm light palettes is still under the 3:1 non-text minimum. That remains this ticket's to decide, and a semantic --color-success token would settle it for all five palettes at once.

The reverse direction improved too: a dark palette pinned on a light-preference OS used to get green-600 (4.55:1 on gruvbox-dark) and now gets green-400 (8.23:1).

Nothing in 5fb9f95 touches OpmlPanel.tsx:149-153 or 204-208. Those have no dark: variant, so the variant change cannot reach them; they are still bright near-white cards on every dark base.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
From ttrb-1im8 (72030ca), for this audit's inventory rather than as a defect: ThemePicker.tsx adds three new text-muted-foreground call sites, two of them at text-xs (12px) -- the base group headings 'LIGHT THEMES'/'DARK THEMES' and the System hint line. That is the smallest text in the app using that token.

Measured, not assumed: muted-foreground sits on --color-background there, not on --color-muted, so Light is 4.74:1 (hsl(0 0% 45.1%) on white) and clears AA for normal text. The 4.35:1 figure the settings spec records for Light is muted-foreground on muted, a different pairing. No new failure, but if this audit tightens the Light muted-foreground token these two are among the sites that move.

No contrast problem surfaced by the swatches themselves: each one is measured against the palette it names in e2e/settings.spec.ts and all five agree exactly.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Audit complete, commit a19e02f. Full inventory below: what was swept, what was measured, what was fixed, what was deliberately left.

SWEEP. Regex over all non-test .ts/.tsx in app/javascript for (a) numbered Tailwind palette utilities, (b) hex and rgb()/hsl() literals, (c) white/black utilities. Found 19 palette-utility occurrences across 7 files (the ticket said 23 across 11; the extra 4 were in test files). All measured in Chromium via Playwright with canvas-resolved sRGB, because getComputedStyle hands Tailwind's palette back in oklch and the theme tokens in hsl, and parsing either as rgb triples silently produces garbage. The first pass of my own harness did exactly that and reported text-green-500 at 14.59:1 on white; the canvas fix brought it to 2.22, which reconciles with the numbers nkhp and lyo3 recorded.

MEASURED, BEFORE (contrast vs each palette's --color-background):

                     Light   Dark  GruvDark  GruvLight  Sepia
  text-green-500      2.22   8.93      6.60       1.94   1.88
  text-amber-500      2.13   9.27      6.86       1.87   1.81
  text-green-600      3.22   6.15      4.55       2.82   2.73
  text-yellow-600     2.94   6.74      4.98       2.57   2.49
  green-600/dk-400    3.22  11.13      8.23       2.82   2.73

Standard held: 4.5:1. These paint 12px text in FeedOrganizer's sync indicator and 14px in OpmlPanel, and 12px is normal text, not large, so 4.5 applies rather than 3:1; meeting 4.5 also subsumes the 3:1 non-text bar for the same tokens as icon fills. Every light-base palette failed. green-500 and amber-500 were already under 3:1 on plain white before the warm palettes existed.

CONFIRMED, the four findings you listed:

(a) OpmlPanel 149-153 and 204-208. Confirmed as the worst item. The fills are bg-yellow-50 at relative luminance 0.965 and bg-green-50 at 0.953, against a Dark page at 0.003: 19.14:1 and 18.91:1. On Gruvbox Dark 14.16 and 13.99. Not 'foreign', a white card. The text inside them was fine (4.72-6.81) precisely because the card is a self-consistent light-theme island; the defect is the island. Now bg-warning/10 and bg-success/10, which measure 1.13-1.21 against the page on every palette, matching the bg-destructive/10 error card three lines above in the same file.

(b) FeedOrganizer's ready indicator. Confirmed at 3.22 / 2.82 / 2.73 after 5fb9f95, as lyo3 recorded. Now text-success, unconditional: 5.65 Light, 8.26 Dark, 6.66 Gruvbox Dark, 6.80 Gruvbox Light, 6.23 Sepia. The dark: variant is gone, which also removes the class of bug lyo3 was fixing rather than re-parameterising it.

(c) Light's muted-foreground. Confirmed 4.35:1 on --color-muted. I fixed the token rather than keeping the exclusion. Justification: the exclusion was load-bearing in a test whose whole job is to stop this, and the fix is a 1.1-point lightness nudge, not a design decision. shadcn's hsl(0 0% 45.1%) = rgb(115,115,115) becomes 44% = rgb(112,112,112), the lightest grey that clears 4.5 on muted. 113 gives 4.478 and misses. Result 4.54 on muted, 4.95 on background (was 4.74). The two 12px call sites 1im8 flagged move from 4.74 to 4.95. The contrast test now covers all five palettes with nothing exempt.

(d) The white in .dark .tts-word-active. Confirmed, and it is worse than a single number suggests, because it is hue-dependent rather than theme-dependent. Swept the accent wheel at 15-degree steps: white on --color-accent-primary is 1.51:1 at hue 60 and under 4.5 at 16 of 24 hues. The same defect was in .dark .search-mark (2.92 at hue 60, 10 of 24 failing) and in BOTH light-base rules, which pair  against  and fail at 11 of 24. The cause is that the accent ramp is fixed-lightness HSL: L holds across the wheel, luminance does not, so a yellow primary is about six times as bright as a blue one at the same L. Fixing only the literal  cannot work, because no single foreground suits both a yellow and a blue background. All four rules now pair  (L 92%) against  (L 20%), opposite ends of the ramp, which are hue-stable: worst case 4.95:1 on dark bases and 7.83:1 on light, at every hue.

  Visual consequence you should know about: on dark bases the TTS highlight goes from a saturated accent block to a dark accent tint ringed in accent-primary-light, which makes it symmetric with the light-base treatment. If you want the vivid fill kept, the alternative is relative colour syntax (oklch(from var(--color-accent-primary) ...)) to flip the text colour off the fill's own lightness. That keeps the look and needs Chrome 119+/Safari 16.4+/Firefox 128+. I did not take it: it is opaque in a stylesheet and carries browser-support risk, and you can have it later without redoing anything.

(e) The 1im8 text-xs sites. Confirmed as inventory, not defects: 4.74:1 was muted-foreground on --color-background, a different pairing from the 4.35 figure. They now sit at 4.95.

NEW, not previously recorded. --color-destructive is painted as a foreground in 29 places and fails on the two stock palettes: 1.98:1 on Dark, 3.76:1 on Light. Gruvbox Dark 4.59, Gruvbox Light 7.48, Sepia 6.36 all pass. shadcn ships --destructive as a fill (white on Dark's rgb(127,29,29) is a healthy 10.02:1 for the Button) and this app uses it as text. Gruvbox Dark's author already noticed and left a comment in the stylesheet saying so. I did NOT fix it: the fix flips the destructive Button on the stock palettes from dark-red-with-white-text to light-red-with-dark-text, which is a design call about a control that appears in every delete confirmation. Filed as ttrb-x7zz (P1) with the numbers and two options. This is the one item where I am leaving something under the bar rather than picking a colour for you.

ALSO FIXED. NibblerLogo's dark:bg-white painted a white disc on Gruvbox Dark's cream page; now dark:bg-foreground, and the e2e logo assertion reads the palette's own foreground instead of the literal rgb(255,255,255) it used to hardcode. ui/badge's destructive variant hardcoded text-white at 3.19:1 on Gruvbox Dark's light red; now text-destructive-foreground (the variant is currently unused, so nothing renders it today; the residual Light shortfall belongs to ttrb-x7zz).

TOKEN VALUES. Each chosen to clear 4.5:1 against its own palette's --color-muted, which is the harder surface on every palette (lighter than background on light bases, darker on dark ones), so the background case and the /10 tints come free.

  palette        --color-success      --color-warning     worst measured
  light          hsl(145 80% 26%)     hsl(40 95% 29%)     4.70 (warning on tint)
  dark           hsl(145 55% 48%)     hsl(42 75% 50%)     6.31
  gruvbox-dark   hsl(105 45% 56%)     hsl(45 65% 55%)     5.35
  gruvbox-light  hsl(115 80% 21%)     hsl(35 95% 24%)     5.66
  sepia          hsl(125 55% 25%)     hsl(30 75% 28%)     5.37

Gruvbox and Sepia get olive/warm-leaning greens rather than the emerald the greyscale pair uses, so success reads as part of the palette instead of an import.

GUARDS. Two, because neither can see what the other does, and the acceptance criterion needs both.

1. e2e/settings.spec.ts, extended rather than duplicated as instructed. The single low-contrast-palettes test becomes one test per palette over 7 token pairs (foreground, muted-foreground x2 surfaces, success x2, warning x2), all five palettes, no exemptions, reported as one labelled row per pair so a failure names the token that dropped. Plus a new test that sweeps the accent hue wheel at 15-degree steps asserting all four highlight rules clear 4.5 at every hue. Both resolve colour through a canvas, so oklch and hsl are compared correctly.

2. app/javascript/lib/themeTokens.test.ts, new, static. This is NOT a second contrast test: the browser test measures tokens and never looks at components, so a component that writes text-green-500 tomorrow is invisible to it. The token set stays perfectly legible while the component ignores it. This one reads the source. Verified two ways: the regex catches all 19 pre-fix occurrences at HEAD, and injecting text-emerald-400 and bg-white into QueuePanel made it fail naming the file and both classes. Documented exceptions carry a reason each and are per-pattern rather than per-file, so excusing a scrim does not also excuse a status colour someone adds later; a third test fails if an exception stops being needed. Exceptions: tag-colors, LabelManager, ScoreButtons, PreferencesPanel's hue slider, accentColors, and the two modal scrims. The common thread for the first three is that each paints a fill and its own foreground together, so legibility is a property of the pair and never of the page behind it.

SUITES, all four run at this commit: bin/rails test 593 runs / 1835 assertions / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skips. npm run test:run 895 passed / 51 files (baseline 891/50; +4 tests in the new guard file). npm run test:e2e 274 passed / 5 skipped (baseline 269/5; +4 from the contrast test becoming per-palette, +1 the hue sweep). bundle exec rubocop 202 files / no offenses. tsc --noEmit clean.

comments.text:
Correction to the previous comment: my shell interpreted backticks, so four words dropped out of paragraph (d). It should read:

"The same defect was in .dark .search-mark (2.92 at hue 60, 10 of 24 failing) and in BOTH light-base rules, which pair accent-primary-lighter against accent-primary-dark and fail at 11 of 24. title: Run e2e/iframe-keyboard-focus.spec.ts once PostgreSQL is available
description:

The new spec e2e/iframe-keyboard-focus.spec.ts has never been executed against the app. bin/e2e-server failed at db:prepare with PG::ConnectionBad (connection to 127.0.0.1:5432 refused); PostgreSQL was not running on iris and starting it needs privileges this session does not have.

So the mechanism is confirmed; what is unconfirmed is the spec's own selectors and timing against the running Rails app.

To do

- Watch in particular: the PATCH /api/v1/preferences that puts the reader in iframe view before goto, the listbox 'Entries' wait in openFirstEntry, and getByText('NibbleRSS') as the focus-mode visibility probe (it relies on the sidebar wrapper collapsing to width 0 with overflow hidden).
- Fix whatever the first run turns up.

Done as part of ttrb-8zv5 (commit 74d277c), now that PostgreSQL is up and bin/e2e-server boots.

title: Entry list stays stale during background polling (loadEntries is selection-driven only)
description:
Discovered while working on ttrb-7ktq. useBackgroundRefresh now keeps the sidebar badges converged with the server, but app/javascript/application.tsx loadEntries() still only reruns when the selection, sort, or filter preferences change. A reader parked on the Fresh list watches the Fresh badge tick up while the list underneath it does not change until they click away and back.

Options: fold the visible list into the same background tick (needs care - a refetch resets selectedEntry to null and would yank the reader's place), or show a non-destructive 'N new articles' affordance that loads on click. The second is probably right for a reading surface.

Note loadEntries currently does setSelectedEntry(null) on every load, so a naive addition to the poll would close the open article every interval.
close_reason: Background probe reports 'N new articles' without reloading the list: the poll never touches entries or selectedEntry, so the open article and scroll position survive, and the affordance hides while a search is active. Commit 2ce57df.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Commit 2ce57df: added app/javascript/hooks/useNewEntries.ts, a background probe that refetches the visible entries query to one side and publishes a count of ids the list does not hold. Nothing writes to entries until the reader clicks the 'N new articles' row EntryList now renders above the list. loadEntries and the probe share one memoized entriesQuery object; its identity doubles as the list identity that invalidates a stale probe.

Verified: vitest 749/749 (42 files, 21 new: 15 in useNewEntries.test.ts, 6+2 in EntryList.test.tsx), tsc --noEmit clean, esbuild build clean. NOT RUN: Rails/Minitest and Playwright E2E - PostgreSQL is not running in this environment. No Ruby or E2E files were touched.

Left ttrb-81wy's request shape alone; this adds one entries request per tick rather than folding into the counters payload, since counters carry no per-list count for an arbitrary feed/category/tag scope.

title: Background tick refetches feeds+categories when /api/v1/counters already carries the unread counts
description:
Discovered while working on ttrb-7ktq. The background refresh tick calls loadFeeds() (api.feeds.list + api.categories.list) purely so per-feed and per-category unread badges stay current, which makes three requests per poll.

GET /api/v1/counters already returns { feeds: {feed_id => unread}, categories: {category_id => unread} } (app/controllers/api/v1/counters_controller.rb), and loadCounters() in app/javascript/application.tsx discards both, keeping only result.virtual. Applying those maps onto the existing feed/category objects would drop the tick to a single request and stop replacing the whole feeds array every 60s (which currently churns object identity for the sidebar and races FeedOrganizer's optimistic edits - the reason the poll is suspended while settings are open).

Full loadFeeds would still be needed for structural change (a feed added or deleted elsewhere), so keep it on an occasional tick or on visibilitychange only.
close_reason: Background tick reuses the counters response for feed/category unread badges; full loadFeeds kept for structural change on visibilitychange and every 10th tick

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Commit b79195e: loadCounters now overlays the feeds/categories unread maps from GET /api/v1/counters via new app/javascript/lib/unreadCounts.ts (applyUnreadCounts: absent id means zero, unchanged array returned by identity so React bails out of the sidebar re-render). useBackgroundRefresh passes a reason ('interval' | 'visible') to its callback; the tick calls loadFeeds only on tab-return and every 10th tick (FEED_RELOAD_EVERY_TICKS), so the steady-state tick is counters + the ttrb-v565 entries probe = 2 requests, down from 4. No Ruby change needed: Feed belongs_to :user, so feeds_controller's per-feed unread_count and the counters group-by are the same scope. Verified with vitest (760 pass, 43 files), tsc --noEmit clean, esbuild build clean. Rails/Minitest and Playwright not run - PostgreSQL is not running in this session.

title: On-demand article summary: magic icon, background job, live broadcast into a callout
description:
Andy wants a triage summary on demand: click a magic icon, a background job asks the local LLM for one paragraph, progress is visible while it runs, and the finished summary is broadcast into the page as a callout segment. Stated purpose: "So I can read one paragraph to determine if the article is worth the rest of my time."

That purpose is a design constraint, not flavour text. This is a should-I-read-this summary, not a replace-the-article summary. The prompt should answer what the claim or news is and what is new about it, in a form that supports a decision to keep reading or move on.

Explicit requirements from Andy:
- On demand only. Nothing is generated until the icon is clicked.
- Background job, not a synchronous request.
- Live in-progress feedback.
- Broadcast the result into the open page rather than polling for it.

What already exists and should be reused
- LlmClient (app/services/llm_client.rb) wraps Ollama /api/generate at http://baru:11434, model gemma4:e4b, both pinned in config/deploy.yml:43-44. StoryAnalyzer, StoryWrapupGenerator and StoryQueryExtractor all instantiate it plainly and are the pattern to follow for a new summarizer service.
- CachedAudio plus GenerateArticleAudioJob plus the entries#audio action (entries_controller.rb:133) are a working precedent for on-demand generation of a derived artifact: a cache model keyed by content_hash, a validity check, a job, and a status-returning endpoint. The summary feature is the same shape with text instead of a file.
- GoodJob is the queue (production.rb:73, execution_mode :external).

What does not exist
- ActionCable is entirely unconfigured. No config/cable.yml, no app/channels, no adapter gem (solid_cache is present, solid_cable is not), no @rails/actioncable in the frontend. The broadcast requirement is new infrastructure, and it is the largest piece of this epic.

Placement note
Andy asked for the icon "to the right of the add to queue button (or in that toolbar line)". The Add to queue button is at EntryContent.tsx:431, inside the article header in a group gated on !isTtsActiveForThisEntry, and inside the non-iframe branch. A button placed literally beside it disappears while TTS is playing and in iframe view. The header toolbar around line 205 is always visible in both views. Recommend the header toolbar; Andy left it open.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Placement decided by Andy: the summary icon goes where the Add to queue button is, in the article header under the title and before the content (EntryContent.tsx:411-441, the mt-3 flex gap-2 row), NOT the always-visible header toolbar. Supersedes the recommendation in the description.

Two consequences to handle in the UI bead rather than relitigate: that row is gated on !isTtsActiveForThisEntry, so the button disappears while TTS plays for the current entry, and the whole block sits in the non-iframe branch, so it is absent in iframe view.

title: Stand up ActionCable: adapter, authenticated connection, and a React consumer hook
description:
Prerequisite for broadcasting anything. ActionCable is entirely unconfigured in this app.

Verified current state
- No config/cable.yml.
- No app/channels directory, so no ApplicationCable::Connection or ::Channel.
- No cable adapter gem. Gemfile has solid_cache (line 39) and good_job (line 40); solid_cable and redis are absent. actioncable 8.1.3.1 appears in Gemfile.lock only because the rails meta-gem depends on it.
- Nothing mounted in config/routes.rb.
- No @rails/actioncable in the frontend and no createConsumer anywhere in app/javascript.

Critical constraint
Production runs GoodJob with execution_mode :external (config/environments/production.rb:74), so jobs execute in a SEPARATE PROCESS from Puma. The cable adapter must therefore be real cross-process pub/sub. The :async adapter is in-process only and would accept broadcasts from the job process that never reach any connected browser, failing silently with no error. Use solid_cable (Postgres-backed, no new service, consistent with the existing solid_cache choice) or Redis. Do not ship :async in production even though it will appear to work in development.

Scope
- Add the adapter gem and its migration.
- config/cable.yml with a development and production configuration.
- app/channels/application_cable/connection.rb with find_verified_user. Auth here is a cookie session: BaseController#current_user reads User.find_by(id: session[:user_id]), so the connection identifies the same way. Reject unauthorized connections.
- app/channels/application_cable/channel.rb.
- Mount the cable server in config/routes.rb.
- Frontend: add @rails/actioncable, create a single shared consumer, and a React hook for subscribing that cleans up on unmount. One consumer for the app, not one per component.

Scope guard: this bead delivers the plumbing and one trivial proof-of-life subscription. The summary channel itself belongs to the sibling bead.

Wider value
This also unblocks a better fix for ttrb-7ktq (sidebar badges never refresh from background ingestion). That bead currently proposes polling or refetch-on-focus because push was unavailable. With cable in place, the feed refresh job can broadcast counter changes directly. Do not expand this bead to do that, but note it there once this lands.

Acceptance criteria
- A browser subscribes, a job in a separate process broadcasts, and the browser receives it. Verified with GoodJob running externally, not inline, since that is the configuration that can fail silently.
- An unauthenticated connection is rejected.
- The subscription is torn down on unmount with no leaked consumers across navigation.
- Development setup is documented in the README or CLAUDE.md, including how to run the cable-capable stack locally.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Adapter decided by Andy: solid_cable. Postgres-backed, no new service, consistent with the existing solid_cache choice.

Three specifics that follow from this repo's existing multi-database setup:

1. REPEAT OF A KNOWN TRAP. config/database.yml production already carries a long comment explaining that the cache database must NOT inherit the primary's url: key, because Rails merges url: on top of the rest of the config hash (DatabaseConfigurations::UrlConfig) and the URL's database name silently overrides database:. When that happened, the cache resolved to the primary, db:prepare found schema_migrations already present, skipped db/cache_schema.rb, and every Rails.cache call raised PG::UndefinedTable at runtime. The cable entry needs the same URL-derivation treatment and its own migrations_paths (db/cable_migrate). The failure signature differs from the cache case: it will not raise on every request, it will fail at subscribe or broadcast time, which is harder to notice. Follow the cache entry's shape exactly and read that comment first.

2. Development has no multi-database configuration at all; config/database.yml development is a single entry. Decide whether cable gets its own development database or shares the primary, and make bin/setup or the docs reflect it.

3. Connection pool. The default block computes max_connections from the larger of Puma's RAILS_MAX_THREADS and GOOD_JOB_MAX_THREADS + 2, with a comment about undersizing showing up as GoodJob checkout timeouts. Solid Cable polls the database from the web process (subscribers) and is written to from the job process (broadcasts), so it adds connection pressure on both sides. Check the pool math still holds before shipping.

title: EntrySummary model: cache summaries on the shared Entry with content_hash invalidation
description:
Storage for generated summaries, mirroring the CachedAudio precedent.

Key design point: summaries are user-independent
Entry rows are SHARED across users via UserEntry (see the class docs on Entry: "Entries are the core content units... shared across users via UserEntry join records to avoid duplicating article content"). A summary of an articles text does not vary by who is reading it. So it attaches to Entry, not UserEntry, and one users click generates a summary every other subscriber gets for free. That is a real efficiency win on a shared local LLM with finite throughput, and it is the opposite of what a per-user design would do, so make the choice explicitly.

Shape, following CachedAudio (app/models/cached_audio.rb)
- belongs_to :entry
- summary text
- content_hash, so a summary can be invalidated when the article content changes. Entry ALREADY maintains a content_hash for update detection, and CachedAudio#valid_for_content? shows the comparison pattern.
- model, recording which LLM produced it. gemma4:e4b today, and OLLAMA_MODEL is a one-line deploy change, so a stored summary should say what generated it. StoryAnalysis may already do something similar; check before inventing a convention.
- generated_at

Table vs columns on entries
A separate entry_summaries table keeps the hot, wide entries table from growing a large text column that is null for the overwhelming majority of rows, and matches how cached_audio and story_analyses already hang off their parents. Recommended. Columns on entries would be simpler but entries is the most-queried table in the app.

Also decide
- Retention. PurgeArticlesJob removes old articles; summaries must not outlive their entries. A dependent: :destroy on the association covers it, but check the purge path actually goes through ActiveRecord and not raw SQL.
- Whether a stale summary (content_hash mismatch) is shown with a note or hidden entirely. Recommend hidden, since a summary of superseded text is worse than none for a triage decision.

Affected files
- new app/models/entry_summary.rb and migration
- app/models/entry.rb (has_one :entry_summary, dependent: :destroy)
- app/jobs/purge_articles_job.rb (verify cascade)

Acceptance criteria
- A summary generated by one user is visible to every other user subscribed to the same entry.
- Editing an entrys content invalidates its summary rather than showing a summary of the old text.
- Destroying an entry destroys its summary.
- Model tests for validity checking and invalidation.

title: EntrySummarizer service: one-paragraph triage summary via LlmClient
description:
The service that builds the prompt and calls the model. Follows StoryAnalyzer, StoryWrapupGenerator and StoryQueryExtractor, which all take llm_client: LlmClient.new in the initializer for test injection.

Prompt goal
Andy: "So I can read one paragraph to determine if the article is worth the rest of my time." This is a triage summary, not a replacement for reading. It should convey what the article claims or reports and what is actually new in it, in a form that supports deciding to continue or move on. It should NOT be a generic abstract that restates the headline in longer words, which is what an unconstrained summarize-this prompt produces.

Requirements
- Plain prose, one paragraph. StoryWrapupGenerator returns prose verbatim and is the closer template; StoryAnalyzer returns JSON and is not.
- Bound the output length explicitly in the prompt AND handle the model ignoring it. A local model will overshoot.
- Cap the input. StoryAnalyzer uses SNIPPET_CHAR_LIMIT 400 and MAX_ARTICLES_IN_PROMPT 30 for the same reason; here the cap is on article length. Strip HTML first (ActionController::Base.helpers.strip_tags is used elsewhere for this, e.g. Entry#update_tsvector and SearchController#generate_snippet).
- Raise a typed error on empty or unusable output, matching StoryWrapupGenerator::WrapupFailed and StoryAnalyzer::AnalysisFailed.
- Record which model produced the summary so the stored row can carry it.

Known limitation to handle: thin content
Many feeds publish only an excerpt, so Entry#content is sometimes a couple of sentences. Summarizing a two-sentence excerpt produces a summary no shorter than the input and tells Andy nothing he did not get from the title. Decide the behaviour: below some content length, refuse and say the article is too short to summarize rather than generating something useless. Fetching the full article text is a separate capability and has its own bead.

Timeout
LlmClient defaults to 120s and warns above 30s. Summarizing one article should be well under a story wrapup, but pick the timeout deliberately rather than inheriting the default, and let the job own retry.

Affected files
- new app/services/entry_summarizer.rb
- new test/services/entry_summarizer_test.rb

Acceptance criteria
- Given an article, returns one paragraph of prose within the stated length bound.
- Content is stripped of HTML and truncated before it reaches the prompt.
- An empty or garbage model response raises a typed error rather than persisting rubbish.
- Below the minimum content length, refuses with a distinguishable result.
- Tests inject a stub client and never hit the network.

title: SummarizeEntryJob and EntrySummaryChannel: enqueue, dedupe, and broadcast progress plus result
description:
The background job Andy asked for, and the broadcast that carries its states to the open page.

Flow
1. POST to an endpoint on the entry (member route alongside the existing audio, info, toggle_read) enqueues the job and returns immediately with the current state.
2. The job broadcasts a running state, calls EntrySummarizer, persists an EntrySummary, and broadcasts the result.
3. On failure it broadcasts a failed state carrying a message the UI can show.

Broadcast states: queued, running, ready (with the summary text), failed (with a reason), and unavailable when the LLM host is unreachable. LlmClient raises LlmClient::Unreachable specifically for a down or timed-out Ollama, and AnalyzeStoryJob and GenerateStoryWrapupJob already retry_on it with polynomially_longer backoff over 3 attempts. Follow that, and only broadcast unavailable once retries are exhausted so a transient blip does not flash an error at the reader.

Channel scoping
Summaries live on the shared Entry, so a summary generated by one user is valid for every other subscriber. Decide whether the channel is per-entry (everyone viewing that entry sees it appear) or per-user. Per-entry is the honest match for shared data and means a second user viewing the same article gets the result without asking. Whichever is chosen, the connection must still verify the subscriber actually has a UserEntry for that entry, or the channel becomes a way to read arbitrary entry ids.

Duplicate suppression
Two clicks, or two users on the same article, must not run the model twice. entries#audio already solves this by querying GoodJob::Job for a recent job with the entry id in serialized_params (entries_controller.rb:160-163). That works but is a string LIKE against a JSON column and is not something to spread further without thought. Consider a state column on entry_summaries, or GoodJob concurrency controls, which exist for exactly this. Pick one and note why.

Depends on the ActionCable plumbing and the EntrySummary model.

Affected files
- new app/jobs/summarize_entry_job.rb
- new app/channels/entry_summary_channel.rb
- app/controllers/api/v1/entries_controller.rb and config/routes.rb (new member route)
- app/javascript/lib/api.ts (the trigger call)

Acceptance criteria
- Clicking twice in quick succession runs the model once.
- Two users viewing the same entry both receive the result from a single generation.
- Ollama being down produces an unavailable state after retries, not an immediate error and not a hang.
- A subscriber without a UserEntry for the entry cannot subscribe.
- Job and channel tests, with the LLM stubbed.

title: Summary UI: magic icon beside Add to queue, live progress, and a callout segment
description:
The visible half. Andy: a "little magic summary icon", giving "a one paragraph summary in a callout segment".

Placement, decided
The icon goes in the article header row that holds Listen and Add to queue, under the title and before the content: EntryContent.tsx:411-441, the mt-3 flex gap-2 div. Andy confirmed this is the right location, not the always-visible header toolbar.

Two consequences of that row, to handle rather than relitigate:
- The row is wrapped in {!isTtsActiveForThisEntry && ...}, so it vanishes entirely while TTS is playing for the current entry. The summary button should not inherit that gating; it has nothing to do with TTS state. Either lift the summary button out of that conditional into its own always-rendered slot in the same row, or restructure the row so only the Listen and queue buttons are gated.
- The whole block sits inside the non-iframe branch, so it is absent in iframe view. That is arguably fine, since in iframe view the article text Nibbler would summarize is not what is on screen. Confirm with Andy or note the decision in code.

Icon
lucide-react is already the icon set (EntryContent.tsx:5). Sparkles or Wand2 is the conventional magic-summary glyph. Match the existing sibling buttons: variant ghost, size icon, h-8 w-8, a title attribute, and an aria-label.

States, driven by the channel
- idle: the icon, clickable.
- queued and running: in-place progress on the button plus a placeholder callout. Andy asked for live in-progress feedback, so a spinner that says nothing is the floor, not the goal. The job broadcasts distinct queued and running states; use them.
- ready: the callout with the paragraph.
- failed and unavailable: a short message in the callout with a retry affordance. Unavailable means the local LLM host is down and is worth wording differently from a generation failure.

Callout segment
Renders between the header and the article content. Visually distinct from the article body so it never reads as part of the piece: use theme tokens (muted, border, accent) rather than literal colours, since new themes are coming (see the theming epic). Must be dismissible, and should say it was machine-generated and by which model. Re-opening an entry with a cached summary shows it immediately without a request.

Affected files
- app/javascript/components/EntryContent.tsx
- app/javascript/lib/api.ts
- the cable subscription hook from the ActionCable bead
- new EntrySummaryCallout component, if it earns its own file

Acceptance criteria
- Nothing is generated until the icon is clicked.
- The button is present regardless of TTS playback state.
- Progress is visible from click to result, distinguishing queued from running.
- The finished paragraph arrives by broadcast with no polling and no page action.
- An entry with a cached summary shows it on open without regenerating.
- The callout is legible in light, dark and any added theme.
- Vitest coverage for each state and for the cached-on-open path.

title: Fetch full article text for entries whose feed only publishes an excerpt
description:
Discovered while scoping the on-demand summary feature. Not required for it, but it caps how useful that feature can be.

Problem
Entry#content holds whatever the feed published, via FeedParser#extract_content (app/services/feed_parser.rb:114). Many feeds publish only a headline and one or two sentences. For those entries:
- The summary feature has nothing to summarize. A one-paragraph summary of a two-sentence excerpt is not shorter than the excerpt and answers no question the title did not already answer. The EntrySummarizer bead handles this by refusing below a length threshold, which is the honest behaviour but leaves the feature unavailable on exactly the feeds where deciding whether to read matters most.
- Full-text search over tsvector_combined indexes title and content only, so excerpt-only entries are close to invisible to the search epic beyond their titles.
- TTS reads the excerpt aloud and stops.

So this one capability lifts the ceiling on three separate features.

Not currently present
No readability or full-text extraction anywhere: no such gem in the Gemfile and no extraction service in app/services. StoryArticle does not do it either.

Considerations
- Politeness and rate limiting. DomainThrottler already exists in app/services and should be reused rather than reinvented.
- Storage. Fetched text is derived data on the shared Entry, same reasoning as EntrySummary. Do not overwrite Entry#content, since content_hash drives update detection and audio and summary invalidation; a separate column or table keeps that intact.
- When to fetch: eagerly at feed refresh (expensive, mostly wasted) or lazily on demand when a feature needs it (slower first use, far less traffic). Lazy fits the on-demand summary shape and is recommended.
- Paywalls and consent. Many sites truncate deliberately. Decide whether a failed or paywalled fetch is silent or surfaced.
- Cache invalidation and purge, matching whatever EntrySummary does.

Acceptance criteria
- An excerpt-only entry can have its full text fetched on demand, stored separately from Entry#content.
- Fetching respects DomainThrottler.
- Summary, search and TTS can opt into using fetched text where present.
- A failed fetch degrades to the excerpt rather than erroring the calling feature.

title: Run embed_policy_probe_test.rb and cover the embed-block fallback in E2E
description:
Discovered during ttrb-watz, which was implemented with PostgreSQL down.

test/services/embed_policy_probe_test.rb (20 examples) has never executed: test_helper's 'fixtures :all' needs the database. The probe logic itself was verified against a real TCPServer through bin/rails runner (20/20 cases, plus caching and route resolution), and the two idioms most likely to be wrong in the Minitest file were checked separately -- faraday-follow_redirects follows a HEAD 302 with HEAD, and Rails.cache= swaps and restores cleanly -- but the file needs one real run.

Also unrun: the controller action GET /api/v1/entries/:id/embed_policy end to end, and any Playwright coverage of the fallback panel. An E2E example would need a fixture entry whose link points at something serving X-Frame-Options; OFFLINE_FEED_FETCH=1 currently short-circuits EmbedPolicyProbe to :unknown, so the suite would need a way past that switch for the one example.
close_reason: main is green again: bin/rails test gives 489 runs, 1439 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips (was 485/12 errors). The 12 errors were one bad helper signature in embed_policy_probe_test.rb, not a service bug. title: Outbound HTTP services have no SSRF guard: user-supplied URLs reach internal hosts, and redirects bypass any first-hop check
description:
A background security review flagged EmbedPolicyProbe (added in ttrb-watz, commit e720e56) for SSRF. The finding is real but it is not new: the probe is the fifth outbound-HTTP service that resolves a user-supplied URL with no destination guard.

Call sites, all Faraday/Net::HTTP with no host validation:
- app/services/embed_policy_probe.rb:158
- app/services/feed_fetcher.rb:125
- app/services/image_cacher.rb:225
- app/services/favicon_fetcher.rb:163
- app/services/google_news_rss_fetcher.rb:101

Threat model, stated plainly so the priority is arguable: the URL originates in a feed the authenticated user subscribed to. On a single-user self-hosted install the attacker would have to be the operator, who already controls the host. That is why this is P1 and not P0. It stops being merely theoretical if Nibbler ever serves more than one account, or if a subscribed feed is itself compromised and starts emitting <link> targets aimed at the host.

Two things make the probe the sharpest of the five:

1. It is reachable synchronously from a request. GET /api/v1/entries/:id/embed_policy triggers the fetch inline, so response timing is an oracle. The others run in background jobs.
2. Result#reason is returned to the client and echoes the failure: "Connection failed: #{e.message}". Open port, closed port, and DNS failure produce distinguishable strings, which is a port-scanning primitive against 127.0.0.1 and the link-local 169.254.169.254 metadata address.

Also note embed_policy_probe.rb:162 sets `f.response :follow_redirects, limit: 5`. A guard applied only to the URL as given is defeated by a public host that 302s to an internal one, so validation has to run on every hop, not just the first. image_cacher and favicon_fetcher follow redirects too.

Sketch: one shared resolver used by all five connections that resolves the hostname and rejects the result when it lands in a private, loopback, link-local, or unique-local range, applied per redirect hop rather than once up front. Faraday middleware is the natural shape since four of the five already build a Faraday connection. Guard against DNS rebinding by pinning the connection to the address that was validated, or accept that gap explicitly and write down why.

Additionally: collapse Result#reason for the :unknown case to a single opaque string before it crosses the API boundary. The detailed message is useful in logs and is exactly the oracle in the response.

Acceptance criteria:
- A feed entry linking to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, or a private-range address is refused by every one of the five services.
- A public host that redirects to an internal address is refused at the redirect hop.
- GET /api/v1/entries/:id/embed_policy returns the same body and comparable timing for a refused-internal target regardless of whether that port is open.
- Existing behavior for ordinary public URLs is unchanged; the feed suite still passes.
- OFFLINE_FEED_FETCH continues to short-circuit before any of this.

Discovered during the ttrb-watz bdexec run. Not fixed there: it is a five-site cross-cutting change, and the run had a no-side-quest contract.
close_reason: Shared destination guard across all five outbound HTTP services, applied per redirect hop, with the connection pinned to the validated address; EmbedPolicyProbe's :unknown reason collapsed to one opaque string. Commit 947a9c1.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Status change: this is now LIVE IN PRODUCTION. Andy deployed 29fbf96 manually with kamal deploy; nibbler-web and nibbler-job are both up on that image on 192.168.1.208.

So GET /api/v1/entries/:id/embed_policy is a reachable production endpoint, and EmbedPolicyProbe is making real outbound HEAD/GET requests from inside the production container on every article opened in iframe view. The two properties that made it the sharpest of the five call sites are no longer hypothetical:

- It is synchronous in a request, so response timing is a live oracle.
- Result#reason crosses the API boundary and distinguishes open port, closed port, and DNS failure by message text.

The threat model is unchanged and still argues against P0: the URL comes from a feed the authenticated operator subscribed to, and this is a single-user self-hosted install on a LAN host that the operator already controls. I am not bumping the priority unilaterally. But 'not yet deployed' was part of why P1 was comfortable, and that part is gone.

One thing worth doing cheaply and immediately, ahead of the full five-site guard: collapse Result#reason to a single opaque string for the :unknown case before it is rendered. That removes the port-scanning oracle without touching the Faraday connections, and it is a few lines in embed_policy_probe.rb rather than the cross-cutting middleware change.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text:
Commit 947a9c1. Both halves in one commit -- the probe's opaque reason and the shared guard touch the same file and the same test file, and splitting them leaves an intermediate commit whose tests do not pass.

Part 1: EmbedPolicyProbe::UNKNOWN_REASON = 'Unavailable' is now the reason on every :unknown result (no link, offline, HTTP nnn, timeout, connection failure, unexpected error). The wording goes to Rails.logger.info. Three existing examples that asserted the old strings now assert they are indistinguishable, plus a controller example that requests embed_policy for 127.0.0.1:5432, 127.0.0.1:1 and 169.254.169.254 and asserts the three response bodies are byte-identical. With the guard in place no socket is opened for any of them, so the timing oracle goes with the wording.

Part 2: app/services/outbound_destination.rb (policy: 18 CIDR blocks, scheme allowlist, getaddrinfo-based name resolution) and app/services/outbound_http.rb (OutboundHttp.connection, Guard middleware, PinnedNetHttp adapter). All five call sites now build their connection through OutboundHttp.connection with their existing timeouts, redirect limits and User-Agent preserved exactly.

Redirect hops: Guard is registered AFTER :follow_redirects. FollowRedirects#perform_with_redirection calls @app.call for each hop, so everything below it re-runs per hop; above it would see the first URL only. Asserted structurally for all five connections and behaviourally for both FeedFetcher and EmbedPolicyProbe (public host 302s to an internal address, refused at the hop).

DNS rebinding: closed, not accepted. PinnedNetHttp sets Net::HTTP#ipaddr to the address the guard validated. Net::HTTP connects the socket to ipaddr while keeping #address for the Host header, the TLS SNI name and the certificate hostname check, so there is exactly one lookup per request and no window between judging and connecting. Verified with a real TLS request to example.com through a pinned connection, not only under WebMock.

Resolution failure allows rather than refuses, deliberately: a name that will not resolve cannot reach anything, and turning it into a refusal would make every dead feed domain a security event. Checked against ttrb-utr5's cases in development with the real resolver -- binjonline.com and flak.tedunangst.com come back ALLOW pin=nil and keep failing on getaddrinfo exactly as before; informationisbeautiful.net, news.ycombinator.com and news.google.com all resolve and pin.

Non-literal spellings of loopback are caught because resolution goes through getaddrinfo, the same call Net::HTTP makes: localhost, 0177.0.0.1 and 2130706433 all refuse in development.

LlmClient: out of scope, decided and written into the OutboundHttp doc comment. It is Net::HTTP against OLLAMA_URL (default http://baru:11434, a LAN host). Nothing user-controlled reaches its URL, and it is precisely the private-range destination the guard refuses, so routing it through this would break it to guard against a threat it does not have.

Test environment: config.x.outbound_http.resolver in config/environments/test.rb resolves nothing, so the suite's invented hostnames never make a real DNS query. Literal addresses are checked with no resolver, so the guard stays live for 127.0.0.1 / 169.254.169.254 / private ranges in both the minitest suite and the offline E2E server. ActiveSupport::TestCase#with_dns swaps in a map for tests that need a name to resolve somewhere specific.

OFFLINE_FEED_FETCH is untouched -- both short-circuits still return before any connection is built.

Counts: bin/rails test 519 runs / 1527 assertions / 0 failures / 0 errors (baseline 489/1439; +30 examples). npm run test:run 790 passed / 45 files. npm run test:e2e 236 passed / 5 skipped / 0 failed. bundle exec rubocop 194 files / no offenses (baseline 190 files; +4 files added).

Not committed: .beads/issues.jsonl, per the run contract.

title: Generate search snippets with ts_headline instead of substring matching
description:
generate_snippet in app/controllers/api/v1/search_controller.rb finds the excerpt with a plain case-insensitive substring match, but the search itself runs through plainto_tsquery, which stems. A hit on a stemmed form (query 'run', article says 'running' -- or worse, query 'running', article says 'run') can therefore return an excerpt with no visible occurrence of the query at all, and the client-side highlighter in app/javascript/lib/searchHighlight.tsx has nothing to mark.

ts_headline does the stem-aware version in Postgres: it picks the excerpt around the actual tsquery match and wraps the matched lexemes in StartSel/StopSel delimiters. Moving to it would replace generate_snippet outright.

Notes
- Return the marked-up structure in a form the client can render without dangerouslySetInnerHTML: either custom StartSel/StopSel sentinels the client splits on, or a pre-split array of {text, match} segments. Do not return raw HTML for the client to inject.
- searchHighlight.tsx currently compensates by anchoring each term at a word start and extending the mark over the rest of the word, which covers 'run' -> 'running' but not the reverse or irregular stems. That fallback can stay as-is or be dropped once the server marks the terms.
- Requires a database to develop and test against; blocked the same way ttrb-soaj is.

Discovered during ttrb-a81x.
close_reason: Snippets now come from ts_headline, so a stemmed hit shows the word that actually matched. Delimiters are control characters the client turns into <mark> React nodes; no server HTML is injected anywhere.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Newly observable after ttrb-voe4, and confirmed with a concrete case. Query 'studies' stems to 'studi' and matches an article containing 'study', so the row IS returned; generate_snippet then runs /studies/i over the plain text, finds nothing, and falls back to the first 200 characters. The user gets a result whose snippet contains no visible reason it matched, and searchHighlight.tsx has nothing to mark. Before ttrb-voe4 no rows came back at all, so this was unreachable.

comments.author: Andy Nutter-Upham
comments.text: Commit 41e4c21: generate_snippet replaced by Entry.text_search_headline (ts_headline over Entry::SEARCH_DOCUMENT_SQL, the same document expression the tsvector_combined generated column uses, with the same tsquery text_search_condition/text_search_rank build). Delimiters are Entry::HEADLINE_START/STOP = U+0002/U+0003, not markup. The client gains highlightHeadline in app/javascript/lib/searchHighlight.tsx, which splits the string on those and builds <mark> React elements; every other character stays a text node React escapes, so dangerouslySetInnerHTML is still absent from the whole path and the property a81x verified survives. An unclosed delimiter renders as text rather than marking to the end of the snippet. highlightTerms is kept, now for the title only, which stays the plain identity field over the wire. ts_headline runs in its own query over the page's entry ids, not in the ranked query's select list, because the target list there is evaluated below the sort. Acceptance test test/controllers/api/v1/search_controller_test.rb:119 failed first with the documented fallback: Expected "Filler about bandicoots. ... Filler about bandicoot..." to include "study".
